routers_note: SwapRouter02. Published by Uniswap for Robinhood Chain, then VERIFIED rather than believed: eth_getCode returns 24497 bytes; factory() returns 0x1f7d7550b1b028f7571e69a784071f0205fd2efa, the same factory the pools in this file come from — derived independently from a pool during the go/no-go test, so the two agree without either having been told the other; and the bytecode carries exactInputSingle (0x04e45aaf), which is the selector this signer builds. A swap using the signer's own calldata was then executed against live state and returned 0.308992 AAPL for 100 USDG, while a control with an impossible minimum reverted — so the simulation is not a no-op. The canonical UniversalRouter address is deliberately NOT here: it exists on this chain and is not wired to this factory (go/no-go condition 5). Uniswap publishes a different UniversalRouter for this chain (0x8876789976decbfcbbbe364623c63652db8c0904); it is not listed either, because a router earns a place here only once the exact calldata this service produces has been proven against it, and the signer produces exactInputSingle.

limits.note:
THE PLATFORM BOUNDS PLATFORM THINGS. An agent is designed by its owner: how large a position to take, how often to trade, how much cost to tolerate. Those are trading style and they are not decided here.

max_trade_notional_usd WAS REMOVED on 2026-09-11. It capped a single trade at $100, which is a statement about how much of their own money an owner may commit to one idea. What actually bounds a swap is real rather than policy: the wallet balance, and the min_out floor the transaction carries into the pool. Nothing in this file caps trade size any more, and nothing should: if a future note suggests lowering a size ceiling, the ceiling it means does not exist.

WHAT REMAINS HERE, and why each is the platform's business rather than the owner's:

max_signatures_per_agent_per_day bounds how much of the PLATFORM's capacity one agent may consume -- nonces, RPC calls, the signer's own throughput. It is not a bound on the owner's money. RAISED FROM 60 TO 1200 ON 2026-09-20, when cadence became the owner's number (agents.cadence_seconds) and the platform default became the floor of 60 seconds. The arithmetic, the same way it was done for 60: an agent looking every minute decides up to 1440 times a day; at the observed one-trade-in-five rate that is ~288 trades; every swap needs a fresh approval because the broker approves exactly the trade amount, so ~576 signatures; TP/SL can fire between decisions, which is the other half of the headroom. 1200 covers that with room, and a cap of 60 would have refused a normally-behaving one-minute agent after about thirty trades -- appearing to its owner as an agent that stopped trading for no stated reason, which is the exact fault this cap must not become. It is still a real ceiling: ~2.4x the modelled worst case, not unbounded, because nonces, RPC calls and this signer's throughput are the PLATFORM's capacity and one agent may not consume all of it. An agent that reaches it is refused with a recorded reason rather than silently skipped.

WHAT DID NOT CHANGE: this is not a bound on the owner's money. How often to trade and how much cost to tolerate are the owner's, set by cadence_seconds and the rebalance band. If a future reader wants to lower this to control spending, it is the wrong lever and always was.

APPROVALS COUNT AS SIGNATURES, and that is deliberate. The alternative is approving more than the trade needs, which leaves an allowance open that a misbehaving router could drain.

max_approve_multiple_of_trade is no longer multiplied by anything and is kept so existing files still load. The approval rule is now structural: the signer refuses an approval of 2^255 base units or more, because that is the infinite-allowance idiom rather than a quantity -- larger than the supply of any token that exists. An unlimited approval is not a large trade, it is a standing right for somebody else to empty the wallet.

The token and router lists, the two intents this signer can build, and the rule that proceeds may only reach the agent's own wallet are the other platform limits. They stop an agent doing something that is not trading. They do not decide how it trades.

blocklist_note: EVERY token here is excepted from isBlocked() and NONE is excepted from paused(). That is not a shortcut: the exception is per-token, carries the payload the chain actually returns, and is re-checked by the signer on every signature. A token whose isBlocked() starts answering is checked normally again the same second, with no file to edit — and one that starts reverting DIFFERENTLY is refused, because the recorded evidence no longer describes it. What is being traded away is failing early and cheaply; a wallet that really is blocked still cannot move funds, because the transfer reverts on chain. The risk is a wasted gas fee, not the principal.
